Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

Section 01: Course Synthesis and Sample Project Walkthrough

Welcome to Module 14, the final course synthesis for IAN 603.

You have now worked through relational design, S Q L querying, aggregation, logic, joins, subqueries, text and date transformation, data cleaning, reshaping, advanced S Q L, reusable views, and distributed processing with Spark.

[tts-break]

This module brings those ideas together into one complete way of thinking about data preparation.

The goal is not to introduce a large new set of commands. Instead, I want you to see how the skills from the course connect when you work on a realistic problem.

We will use a small public-transit example from Greensboro to walk through the process. We will inspect the source, identify quality issues, clean only what we can justify, integrate tables carefully, validate the final result, and document the decisions.

One important point before we begin: this walkthrough is a sample. It is not the official Final Project assignment. Your actual Final Project instructions, rubric, required files, due date, and submission area are in Canvas.


Section 02: Module Contents

Here is the overall path for this module.

We begin by clarifying the role of this page and the role of Canvas. Then we connect the major course skills into one workflow.

After that, we use a small transit example to move through profiling, cleaning, normalization, integration, validation, and documentation.

At the end, you will use a readiness checklist and a few reflection questions to prepare for your own Final Project.

Think of this module as a bridge between learning individual techniques and applying them as one defensible process.


Section 03: This module is a synthesis, not the final-project assignment

Module 14 is a synthesis.

That means we are combining the ideas from Modules 1 through 13 rather than treating this page as the official project prompt.

Across the semester, you learned many techniques separately. You learned how to understand structure, write queries, combine tables, clean values, reshape data, build reusable logic, and think about scale.

Now we are asking a bigger question: how do those skills work together when the data is messy and the final output must be trustworthy?

The sample on this page helps answer that question. Your own Final Project may use different data, different requirements, and different deliverables.


Section 04: Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you should be able to explain an end-to-end data-preparation workflow.

You should be able to identify which course techniques belong at different stages of that workflow.

You should also be able to look at a sample project and discuss its data-quality risks, transformation decisions, output grain, and validation evidence.

Most importantly, you should be able to separate a teaching example from the actual assignment requirements.

When you prepare your own Final Project, you should use Canvas as the source of truth and use the ideas from this module as a reasoning framework.


Section 05: Your actual final project is in Canvas

Your actual Final Project is in Canvas.

This page is here to help you think through the process, but it does not replace the Canvas assignment.

When you are ready to begin your project, go to the Final Project area in Canvas and read the complete instructions before choosing your approach.

That will prevent a common problem: building a good project that does not actually match the required deliverables.


Section 06: Canvas is the authoritative location

Canvas is the authoritative location for the Final Project.

Use Canvas for the official prompt, the grading rubric, the required files, the due date, formatting requirements, and submission instructions.

If anything on this sample page seems different from Canvas, follow Canvas.

The sample here teaches the workflow. Canvas defines what you must submit.


Section 07: Instructions

Before you choose a dataset or begin writing code, read the entire Final Project assignment in Canvas.

Do not start from assumptions.

First understand what the assignment is asking you to produce, how it will be graded, and what evidence you need to include.

That is the same principle we use in data preparation: understand the requirement before transforming the data.


Section 08: Rubric

Use the Canvas rubric as a quality-control checklist.

Do not wait until the end to look at the rubric.

Read it early, and then use it again before submission.

A rubric tells you what evidence the instructor expects to see. That can help you decide what to document, what screenshots or outputs to preserve, and what explanations need to be clear.


Section 09: Submission

When your project is complete, submit the required materials through Canvas.

After uploading, verify that the submission was successful and that the correct files are attached.

This sounds simple, but it is part of a professional workflow. A completed project that is not submitted correctly cannot be evaluated.

So treat submission verification as the final validation step for the assignment itself.


Section 10: How the course skills fit into one workflow

A real data-preparation project rarely follows the course modules in a perfect straight line.

You may inspect the data, notice a quality problem, return to the schema, clean a field, join another source, discover a grain problem, reshape the output, and then validate again.

[tts-break]

A useful workflow is to think in stages.

First, understand the context and the meaning of one row.

Second, profile the data and identify problems.

Third, clean and standardize only what you can justify.

Fourth, integrate sources using correct keys and cardinality.

Fifth, transform the structure for the analytical goal.

Finally, validate and communicate what you did.

You may move back and forth between these stages, but each decision should remain explainable.


Section 11: Meaning and structure

The first part of the course focused on meaning and structure.

Before writing complex S Q L, you need to understand data types, keys, relationships, quality dimensions, and normalization.

For example, if one table has one row per patient and another has many admissions per patient, that relationship affects every later join.

A technically correct query can still be analytically wrong if the row meaning is misunderstood.

So the first question in almost every project should be: what does one row represent?


Section 12: Relational querying

The next group of skills involved relational querying.

You learned how to select data, modify data, aggregate values, apply Boolean logic, join tables, and use subqueries.

These are not isolated commands. They are tools for changing the grain and combining information.

For example, a join can add useful attributes, but a one-to-many join can also multiply rows.

An aggregate can summarize information, but it can also remove detail.

The important habit is to understand what each query changes about the result.


Section 13: Preparation and shape

Modules 8 through 10 focused heavily on preparation and analytical shape.

You worked with strings, dates, validation, cleaning, duplicate detection, pivoting, and un pivoting.

These skills are useful because real data rarely arrives in the exact form we want.

But cleaning does not mean forcing every value into a convenient form.

Sometimes the correct action is to standardize. Sometimes it is to flag. Sometimes it is to preserve a null value because the truth is unknown.

And when reshaping, we always protect the meaning of the data by checking grain and totals.


Section 14: Reusable and scalable analytics

Modules 11 through 13 moved toward reusable and scalable analytics.

You learned common table expressions, window functions, standard views, materialized views, modular design, Spark S Q L, and distributed execution.

These tools help when the logic becomes larger, when many people need the same definition, or when the amount of data grows.

Even in those more advanced environments, the basic habits do not change.

You still need clear grain, trustworthy joins, careful null handling, validation, and documentation.


Section 15: Sample project: Greensboro public transit data preparation

Now we will use a small Greensboro public-transit example.

Imagine that an analyst receives three C S V files.

One file describes bus routes. One describes bus stops. And one contains daily ridership.

The goal is to prepare these sources for analysis.

This is intentionally a small example. The purpose is not to build a complete transit system model. The purpose is to practice the reasoning process from raw source to validated analytical output.


Section 16: bus routes C S V

The first file contains bus routes.

Each route has an I D, a route name, and a field containing major street names.

The important issue is that the street field contains several street names inside one cell, separated by commas.

That may be convenient in a source file, but it is not ideal if we want to analyze streets individually.

So later, we will normalize that field into one route-and-street relationship per row.


Section 17: bus stops C S V

The second file contains bus stops.

Each stop has its own I D, a route I D, a stop name, and an accessibility value.

Some accessibility values are missing.

That creates an important data-quality question.

A missing value does not automatically mean no.

It means we do not know from the source.

So our cleaning process should preserve that uncertainty instead of inventing an answer.


Section 18: daily ridership C S V

The third file contains daily ridership.

Each row has a ridership I D, a route I D, a service date, and a rider count.

The main issue is that the date appears in more than one text format.

For example, one row may use month, day, year with slashes, while another uses year, month, day with hyphens.

Before analysis, we want one consistent typed date column.

The key is to support formats we understand and leave unsupported values as null rather than guessing.


Section 19: What is visibly wrong or risky in the sample?

Even this small sample already contains several risks.

The route file stores multiple street names in one field.

The stop file contains missing accessibility values.

The ridership file contains more than one date representation.

[tts-break]

Notice that none of these problems should be fixed blindly.

The street list needs normalization.

The missing accessibility value should remain unknown unless a trustworthy rule tells us otherwise.

And the date text should be parsed only when it matches a supported format.

This is the difference between cleaning and guessing.


Section 20: Profile before changing anything

Before changing the data, profile it.

Start with basic questions.

How many rows are there?

Are the identifiers unique?

How many route I Ds are missing?

How many rider counts are missing?

What are the minimum and maximum rider counts?

What date formats actually appear in the source?

[tts-break]

Profiling gives you evidence.

If you later explain that you standardized two date formats, you should be able to show that those two formats were actually present.

A cleaning decision is much easier to defend when it is connected to something you observed.


Section 21: Clean values without inventing facts

Once the problems are understood, begin cleaning.

The rule is simple: standardize representation without inventing facts.

For the ridership data, we can convert supported date strings into a typed date.

For accessibility, we can map known yes values to true and known no values to false.

If the source is missing or unclear, we keep a null value.

For the route street list, we can split the known comma-separated values into separate rows.

Each of those changes is explainable because it is based on observed source structure.


Section 22: Standardize date text into a typed date

The date-cleaning query checks the text before converting it.

If the value looks like year, month, day, it is converted directly to a date.

If it looks like month, day, year with slashes, we parse it using that pattern.

If it matches neither supported pattern, the cleaned date becomes null.

[tts-break]

Notice what we are not doing.

We are not trying several random conversions until something works.

We are explicitly stating which formats we support.

That makes the rule easier to test, document, and trust.


Section 23: Normalize accessibility while preserving uncertainty

Now consider the accessibility field.

If the source says yes, we store true.

If it says no, we store false.

If the source is blank, missing, or something we do not recognize, we store null.

We can also create a small status field that tells us whether the source value was present.

This is useful because the cleaned Boolean value and the source-quality status answer different questions.

One describes the normalized value. The other describes what evidence was available.


Section 24: Normalize the comma-separated street list

The route file contains several streets inside one field.

We can split that field at the commas and return one street name per row.

For example, if Route A contains Main Street, Elm Street, and Oak Avenue, the normalized result has three rows for Route A.

This is a better structure if we want to count streets, join street information, or analyze route coverage.

The important idea is not the exact regular-expression syntax. The important idea is that repeated values stored inside one cell can often be normalized into separate rows.


Section 25: Integrate at the correct grain

Now we combine the cleaned data.

Suppose our final analytical grain is one row per route and service date.

Ridership already fits that idea reasonably well.

Stops do not. A route can have many stops.

If we join each ridership row directly to every stop, the rider count repeats once for each stop.

That would inflate later totals.

[tts-break]

So we first summarize stops to one row per route.

For each route, we can calculate the number of stops, the number known to be accessible, and the number with unknown accessibility.

Then we join that route-level summary to the route-and-date ridership data.

This preserves the intended final grain.


Section 26: Validation turns looks clean into evidence

A result can look clean and still be wrong.

Validation gives us evidence that the transformation behaved as intended.

We can test identifier uniqueness.

We can test whether route references are valid.

We can look for dates that failed parsing.

We can check for negative rider counts.

And we can confirm that the final output contains no duplicate route-and-date combinations.

Validation is not one magic query.

It is a collection of checks tied to the properties that matter for the dataset.


Section 27: Uniqueness

A uniqueness check asks whether an identifier appears more than once when it is supposed to be unique.

For ridership, we can group by ridership I D and look for counts greater than one.

If the query returns no rows, that is evidence that we did not find duplicate ridership identifiers.

Be careful with the wording.

An empty result does not prove that the entire dataset is correct.

It only tells us that this specific uniqueness problem was not found.


Section 28: Referential integrity

Referential-integrity validation checks whether related identifiers actually point to valid parent records.

For example, every route I D in the ridership table should match a route in the route table.

A left join can help us find ridership rows that have no matching route.

If any appear, we have an orphaned reference that should be investigated.

This kind of check is essential whenever several source tables are integrated.


Section 29: Date parsing

A date-parsing validation is straightforward.

After creating the cleaned date field, search for rows where that date is null.

Those rows deserve review.

Some may represent missing source dates.

Others may contain unsupported or invalid text.

The important point is that the failed conversion remains visible.

We did not silently replace it with a guessed date.


Section 30: Range validity

Range validation asks whether a numeric value falls inside a reasonable domain.

For rider counts, a negative value is suspicious because a count should not normally be below zero.

That does not automatically tell us what the correct value should be.

It tells us that the record needs review.

This is the same principle you practiced earlier: validation identifies a problem; it does not give us permission to invent a correction.


Section 31: Validate the intended final grain

One of the most important validation checks is the final grain.

If one row is supposed to represent one route on one service date, then the combination of route I D and service date should appear only once.

We can group by those two fields and search for groups with more than one row.

If none are returned, we have evidence that the intended route-by-date grain is unique.

[tts-break]

Again, this validates one property.

We still need the other quality checks as well.


Section 32: Document decisions, not just code

Professional data preparation includes documentation.

Another analyst should be able to understand what the source meant, what you changed, what you deliberately left unchanged, and how you validated the output.

Code alone is not always enough.

A query may show how a value was transformed, but it may not explain why that transformation was appropriate.

Good documentation connects the technical step to the reasoning behind it.


Section 33: What the source meant

Begin documentation with the source.

Describe where the files came from, what the important fields mean, and what one source row represents.

Mention known limitations and assumptions.

For example, if a ridership row represents one route on one day, state that clearly.

Source meaning is the foundation for every later transformation.


Section 34: What you changed

Next, document the transformations.

Explain which text values were standardized.

Explain which types were converted.

Explain whether duplicates were removed or only flagged.

Describe normalization, joins, derived fields, and any change in grain.

A useful question is: could someone understand the purpose of the transformation without reading every line of S Q L?


Section 35: What you refused to guess

Good documentation should also explain what you refused to guess.

Maybe an accessibility value was missing.

Maybe a date did not match a supported pattern.

Maybe two records looked like possible duplicates but there was not enough evidence to merge them.

Those uncertainties should remain visible.

A trustworthy workflow is not one that makes every field look complete.

It is one that distinguishes known values from unknown ones.


Section 36: How you validated it

Finally, document the validation evidence.

Show the checks you used for row counts, keys, ranges, null values, categories, duplicates, referential integrity, and final grain.

If a check returns no problem rows, say what that means.

If a check identifies exceptions, explain how they were handled.

[tts-break]

The goal is reproducibility.

Another analyst should be able to follow the path from source, to transformation, to validation and understand why the final dataset can be trusted.


Section 37: Final-project readiness checklist

Before submitting your Final Project, perform a final review.

First, confirm that you read the complete Canvas prompt and rubric.

Make sure you are not using this transit example as the assignment specification.

Confirm that you can state the grain of each important source and final table.

Check that you profiled the source before cleaning and that your cleaning rules respond to observed issues.

Make sure source values remain traceable where appropriate.

Confirm that you validated the final dataset and that your explanation matches what your code actually produces.

[tts-break]

Then return to Canvas.

Check the required files, file names, due date, and submission instructions.

Upload the project and verify that the correct files were successfully submitted.


Section 38: Course closure: from S Q L syntax to defensible data preparation

As we close IAN 603, remember that the goal of the course is larger than memorizing S Q L commands.

You have practiced making decisions about data meaning, structure, quality, joins, grain, transformation, validation, reuse, and scale.

Those decisions are what make data preparation valuable.

Syntax helps us express the decisions, but the quality of the analysis depends on whether the decisions are correct and explainable.

That is the larger skill I want you to carry forward.


Section 39: A useful final mental model

Here is a useful final mental model.

Correct syntax is necessary, but it is only the beginning.

A strong data-preparation workflow should also be explainable.

It should be reproducible.

It should include validation.

It should preserve uncertainty when the source does not support a confident correction.

It should use a structure that fits the analytical purpose.

And another person should be able to understand how the final result was created.

That is what makes a dataset defensible.


Section 40: Reflection prompts

Before moving to the Final Project, reflect on what changed in the way you think about data.

Which concept from the course changed your approach the most?

Where are you now more likely to check grain before trusting a result?

Which validation query do you think you will use in many future projects?

When would you choose Postgres, and when might Spark or Microsoft Fabric be more appropriate?

And for your Final Project, what evidence will you include to show that your final output is trustworthy?

These questions are not just about the course. They are useful habits for real analytical work.


Section 41: Next action

Your next action is to open the Final Project assignment in Canvas.

Read the official requirements carefully.

Use the Canvas rubric to guide your work.

Apply the course habits you have practiced: understand the source, state the grain, profile before cleaning, avoid guessing, validate the output, and explain your decisions.

[tts-break]

Then submit the required project materials through Canvas and verify the submission.

That completes Module 14 and brings the course together around one central idea: good data preparation is not only about producing an answer. It is about producing an answer that can be understood, checked, and trusted.
